analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to give laid-off workers severance, health coverage, and retraining when jobs move to low-wage countries, and expands plant-closing notice rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 1993 with no cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House committee and died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers that close a plant or lay off workers because the work is moved to a country with much lower wages or weaker labor laws to give affected employees notice 180 days in advance, severance pay worth four weeks of wages per year worked, continued health coverage for 18 months, up to $10,000 for retraining and relocation, and boosted retirement credits. Companies that failed to comply would be barred from federal contracts for those products. It would also expand the existing plant-closing warning law (WARN) to cover smaller employers, triple the advance notice period, and make it easier for workers to sue for back pay and damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose plants close or who are laid off because their jobs move to a low-wage country would get long advance notice, severance pay scaled to their years of service, 18 months of continued health insurance, retraining and relocation money, and accelerated retirement benefits. Communities and states could also recover economic development subsidies paid to companies that later moved the jobs overseas. The expanded WARN coverage would extend 180-day advance notice to employees at smaller plants (50 or more employees) facing closings or layoffs of 25 or more workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at plants closed or downsized by offshoring

how_it_helps.text: Employers closing or downsizing a plant because work moves to a low-wage country would owe each displaced worker severance of four weeks' pay per year of service, 18 months of continued group health coverage, up to $10,000 for retraining, job search, and relocation, weekly training incentive payments, and pension credits as if the worker had stayed five more years [S3].

Employers would have to give 180 days' advance written notice to affected workers and to state and local officials, including the reasons for the closing, the site's profitability, and any alternatives considered [S3].

Companies that violated the notice and benefit requirements could not win federal contracts for the affected or similar products, and states or local governments could sue to claw back tax incentives given to a company that later moved the jobs [S3].

The bill would lower WARN Act coverage thresholds to employers of 50 (from 100) and layoffs of 25 (from 50), lengthen required notice from 60 to 180 days, add interest and doubled liquidated damages, and make attorney's fees mandatory for prevailing workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that shift work to low-wage countries would bear the direct cost: severance, 18 months of health premiums, retraining and incentive payments, funded into worker-managed benefit accounts, plus exposure to doubled liquidated damages and attorney's fees in lawsuits. Companies would also face longer and more detailed notice obligations, and smaller manufacturers newly covered by WARN would owe 180 days' notice before closings or layoffs. Some of these costs could reduce hiring or acceleration of automation at affected firms, and federal contracting firms that violate the rules would lose eligibility for related contracts.

drawbacks.text: The benefit package is expensive per worker: severance of four weeks' pay per year of service plus 18 months of health coverage plus up to $10,000 in retraining could cost an employer tens of thousands of dollars per laid-off employee, which smaller firms might struggle to fund [S3].

Tripling the WARN notice period to 180 days and doubling damages (with liquidated damages at two times back pay plus interest) would raise litigation risk and compliance costs for employers even outside true offshoring cases, and could make firms more cautious about expanding US operations [S2].

The bill does not stop offshoring; it taxes it. A company that judges the required benefits cheaper than the wage savings could still move the work and pay the mandated severance, leaving workers retrained but not re-employd in comparable jobs.
The debarment remedy bars federal contracts only for products involved in or similar to the transferred work, and includes a national security waiver, limiting its bite [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and communities hit by offshoring, the bill offers substantial, concrete compensation: long notice, severance, health coverage, and retraining money at a moment when families otherwise face sudden income loss. The costs fall on a narrower group, employers that relocate work abroad, and would likely be passed into prices or location decisions. The honest objection is that the bill compensates dislocation rather than preventing it, and its heavy damages and notice burdens on all covered employers would carry real compliance costs; whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on protecting workers against sudden, foreseeable dislocation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to a subcommittee in November 1994, and it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. William D. Ford of Michigan introduced the American Jobs Protection Act on May 27, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no action for more than a year; on November 15, 1994, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, near the end of the Congress [S5].
The bill never advanced to a committee vote or the House floor, and expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1].

The bill's stated purpose was to discourage transferring work to low-wage countries and to make companies that do so pay for the dislocation to workers and communities, in the context of the pending NAFTA debate [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move production to low-wage countries are better off, because they never had to fund the required severance, health coverage, and retraining accounts, and smaller employers remain outside the expanded notice rules. Dislocated workers gained nothing from this bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. William D. Ford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 27, 1993 and was its only sponsor; it was referred to the committee he led

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it sat for over 17 months before being sent to a subcommittee on November 15, 1994, with no markup or vote

against.name: House Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations
against.role: Subcommittee that received the referral in November 1994
against.what_they_did: Received the bill weeks before the Congress ended and took no action on it

against.name: US business and manufacturing interests
against.role: Employers subject to the notice, severance, and contract-debarment requirements
against.what_they_did: The bill would have imposed severance, health coverage, and 180-day notice costs on companies closing or downsizing plants in connection with moving work to low-wage countries, and barred violators from related federal contracts

sides.party_line_note: Only one member sponsored the bill and none cosponsored it, and it never reached a vote, so no partisan breakdown of support or opposition exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to fund severance, 18 months of health coverage, and retraining accounts for workers displaced when work moves to a low-wage country, and barred violators from related federal contracts. Their cost is the workers' compensation, so the industry's interest in the bill runs against the workers it lays off. [S3]
Companies that failed to provide the required notice or benefits could not contract with the United States for the affected or similar products, a new compliance-linked eligibility risk. [S3]
Lowering WARN coverage to employers of 50 and layoffs of 25 would have brought many smaller firms under advance-notice law for the first time, with a much longer 180-day notice period. [S2]

industries.industry: Employment litigation and workforce development/training providers
industries.note: Mandatory attorney's fees, expanded damages, and up to $10,000 per worker in retraining and relocation reimbursement would have created paid work for training providers, relocation services, and lawyers representing laid-off workers. [S3]
